title: ‘I, Addict’ Creator Javier Giner Unpacks ‘This Solitude,’ a Film ‘About ‘Those Who Keep Functioning While Something Inside Them Is Falling Apart’
full_text: Oct 5, 2026 11:09am PT ‘I, Addict’ Creator Javier Giner Unpacks ‘This Solitude,’ a Film ‘About ‘Those Who Keep Functioning While Something Inside Them Is Falling Apart’ 'I wanted to take risks, try new forms, trust more in silence and what happens off-screen. I didn’t want to explain the characters psychologically, but to observe them. Where 'I, Addict' screamed, 'This Solitude' whispers,' says Giner By Roberto Prieto Plus Icon Roberto Prieto Latest Produced by J.A. Giner is the creator and co-director of the Disney+ series “I, Addict,” based on his autobiographical book by the same name. It earned lead actor Oriol Pla the International Emmy for Best Actor. Also starring Pla, “This Solitude” follows Leo and Lorea after their five-year relationship has ended. Each of them has to figure out how to continue living life on their own in Bilbao. Leo is a struggling actor who has to work as a grocery clerk to make ends meet while taking care of his disabled father. Lorea is a troubled writer who looks to a former prison inmate for companionship. Both must confront their loneliness and unresolved issues and look for meaning in a world that can sometimes feel cruel and scary. Related Stories ‘The Influencer Project’ Review: Found Footage Terror Takes a Tepid Danish Holiday ‘Vintage Violence’ Review: Cole Sprouse Heads Up a Hyper-Online Gonzo Freakout in Japan Oriol Pla in ‘This Solitude’ “The film is about people who are losing control of their lives. Loneliness may be one of the few truly democratic things in life; what isn’t democratic are the resources we have to survive it,” Giner told Variety . Popular on Variety The film stars Pal, Marina Salas (“Join Me for Breakfast”), Gemma Martínez, Kai Etxaniz and Itziar Lazkano. Giner co-wrote the film with Luisa Matienzo, who is also one of the film’s producers along with Miguel Torrente. The production companies are Balance Media Entertainment, Fuga de Cuerpos, La Embajada TV and Basajaun Filmak. International sales are being handled by Filmax and they will release the film theatrically in Spain on Oct. 30. Director Javier Giner, ‘This Solitude’ Photo Credit: David Herranza Variety interviewed Javier Giner after the film’s premiere in San Sebastián. There is a loneliness epidemic around the world and this film seems to address it. Javier Giner: I didn’t set out to make a film about the loneliness epidemic. I’m a little wary of starting a film with a theme. This began with the desire to create, more than a film, an emotional state that would stay with the audience after they left the theater. I looked around me and saw people with apparently full lives — jobs, friends, partners, phones that never stop, social media — and yet they were profoundly lonely and exhausted. I was fascinated by the contradiction: we’ve never had so many tools to avoid being alone and, paradoxically, so many ways of never truly connecting with anyone. Is this story also autobiographical like your book “I, Addict”? Giner: Everything I write is autobiographical in some way, but not in the sense that “I, Addict” was, where I was explicitly telling the story of a period in my own life. In “Esta Soledad,” the autobiography is in the gaze and in the emotions: Sadness, family relationships, certain ways of loving, the fear of losing someone, the feeling of not knowing what to do with your life. More and more, what interests me is whether what I write is emotionally true. To me, that is a deeper form of autobiography, and something I find endlessly fascinating. The film is also about absent parents, both physically and emotionally. Do you think this is especially true for the new generation? Giner: I think every generation inherits from the previous one not only its traumas, but also its emotional vocabulary, including the things it never had words for. The parents in “Esta Soledad” are not monsters. Even when they cause pain, they love their children and they do the best they can. But loving someone and knowing how to love someone are two very different things. Children end up living with the emotional consequences of decisions they never made. I think we all spend part of our lives trying to understand what we received from our parents, and another part deciding what we’re going to do with it. You chose to work with Oriol Pla again after “I, Addict.” Giner: Oriol and I have something more valuable than simply understanding each other: we trust each other completely. And trust allows for things that are far more interesting and profound than comfort. After “I, Addict,” we had already gone through some very emotionally demanding places together, so now we can arrive on set and barely need to talk. Sometimes a word or a look is enough. Or I can simply tell him, “I don’t know exactly what I’m looking for. Let’s find it together.” Oriol can be explosive, physical, unpredictable, almost animalistic, and five seconds later he can do something tiny that breaks your heart. Very few actors can inhabit both of those extremes. As an actor, he’s a Stradivarius, and on top of that he’s an incredible human being. He’s my brother, my partner. Bilbao seems to be a central character in the film, sometimes portrayed as lonely, dark and gritty. Would you agree? Giner: Yes, although I never wanted to film Bilbao as a sad city, but rather as a state of mind. I wanted to film what almost never gets filmed anymore: not the postcard, but the humidity, the noise, the architecture, the industrial memory, that light that can change completely within a matter of minutes. There is something very physical about the city; at times, it almost seems to weigh on the bodies. That connected with Leo and Lorea. Their external world remains exactly where it was while everything inside them has changed completely. The streets are the same, but they no longer mean the same thing. I believe strongly in that: Cities don’t change when we suffer; the way we look at them does. So Bilbao wasn’t there to illustrate their sadness. It had to remain indifferent to it. And paradoxically, that indifference is what ultimately makes the city so deeply emotional. title: Versailles Gives ‘Marie Antoinette’ (and Sofia Coppola) the Royal Treatment 20 Years Later
full_text: × Skip to main content By Stephanie Sporn Plus Icon Stephanie Sporn View All October 5, 2026 11:05am Kirsten Dunst and Sofia Coppola behind the scenes on Marie Antoinette Andrew Durham When Sofia Coppola was granted access to the Château de Versailles’ hallowed halls for her 2006 film, Marie Antoinette , their collaboration was unprecedented. Though the film initially received criticism for its unconventional portrayal of the young French queen (intentionally opting for an anachronistically stylish over stuffily period-appropriate approach), 20 years later, its legacy is undeniable. This fall the anniversary is being fêted with a new documentary on the movie’s making (directed by Coppola’s late mother, Eleanor), a book featuring behind-the-scenes photographs by Andrew Durham, who also produced her first short movie, Lick the Star (1998), as well as a theatrical re-release in the United States. Now the palace itself is joining in on the fun, too. Related Stories Music Carly Rae Jepsen on How Sofia Coppola's 'Marie Antoinette' and an Overdue Vacation Inspired Her New Single "Versailles" Movies 'Making Marie Antoinette' Review: Eleanor Coppola's Chronicle of Daughter Sofia Shooting Her 2006 Biopic Makes for a Sublime Collaboration of Talents Conceived in collaboration with Coppola and sponsored by Cartier, the Château de Versailles is staging an exhibition about the film’s fascinating origin, painstaking production and cultural impact. On view through January 24, 2027, the show is situated in the Petit Trianon, where Marie Antoinette would seek refuge from the demands of court life and spend time with her closest friends in and among its surrounding gardens. “The strength of the film is how it remains so modern; it seems as if it has been shot yesterday,” Laurent Salomé, Director of the National Museum of the Châteaux de Versailles and Trianon, told The Hollywood Reporter at the exhibition’s press preview last month. Salomé, who co-curated the exhibition with Hélène Delalex, Chief Heritage Curator in Charge of Marie Antoinette’s Apartments, believes much of the film’s timelessness and relatability stems from Coppola’s unique point of view: “Her style is to focus on facial expression and silent moments. It’s about being, suffering, and hoping.” The Billiards Room focuses on the film’s hair and makeup Stephanie Sporn Delalex also praised Coppola’s interpretation of the tragic figure, who was just 14 when she arrived at Versailles and 18 when crowned queen: “As a specialist, I think Sofia Coppola’s intimate portrait of the queen is very accurate in many aspects, for example, her youthful spirit, grace, sincerity, and légèreté , meaning frivolity.” In one of the exhibition’s introductory wall texts, Coppola explains how much of her coming-of-age portrayal of the young dauphine and later queen can be owed to Antonia Fraser’s 2001 biography, Marie Antoinette: The Journey , which offered a more human, sympathetic perspective on its often misunderstood, villainized protagonist. However, the film’s candy-colored palette (derived from a box of macarons ), New Romantic–heavy soundtrack, and countless contemporary winks (eagle-eyed fans will spot those lilac Converse sneakers in the exhibition) are singlehandedly Sofia. “I didn’t think it was so far out to put modern music in that period, and [it’s] cool to see that’s totally accepted by an audience today, and also that a female point of view is accepted as something not unusual,” Coppola told THR . The director added it’s been “fun and gratifying” to see how the film’s legacy endures (even garnering a new generation of fans, including her daughters’ friends). It was also “moving” for her to return to Versailles with leads Kirsten Dunst and Jason Schwartzman on the occasion of this exhibition. “People had been hard on Kirsten when the film came out, and she felt bad that she had let me down. I always loved her performance, so it’s nice to hear people expressing that too.” Coppola had a strong hand in realizing the Versailles exhibition. “At the beginning we had imagined a more classical scenography, but Sofia and [production designer] Scott Dougan wanted it to feel like a teenager took over,” said Delalex, calling Coppola’s working style “delicate, natural, and intuitive.” At the same time, the collaborators sought to reveal the great lengths Coppola’s team went to make the movie possible. The nearly six months of negotiating with Versailles resulted in a major logistical operation. From January to April 2005, the film was shot over 57 days, including 20 days at Versailles. As filming was only allowed on Mondays under strict restrictions, Coppola’s team reconstructed some of the château’s key interiors, such as the Queen’s Grand Chamber and the Royal Opera, in nearby châteaux, such as Millemont. The Main Dining Room recreates the film’s lengthy feasts Stephanie Sporn “I hope [the exhibition] gives an impression a little of what it was like on set and the work that went into it from all the departments,” said Coppola, who provided the curators with original references, mood boards, scene sketches, annotated scripts, casting sheets, hair and makeup test photos, and more. “The curators really wanted to show the film making process, which I thought was so unusual to do at Versailles.” The curators additionally tapped the vast collections of Marie Antoinette ’s production designer, K. K. Barrett, and Supervising Art Director, Anne Seibel. “We discovered hundreds and hundreds of boxes full of memories, papers, and objects [from research binders and sketches to scale models and fabric samples] that are testimonials of the way that almost everything in this film was crafted by hand,” recalled Delalex. Even if it was only featured “for a second and a half,” no detail was overlooked in order to maintain continuity between the real and reconstructed châteaux. The exhibition also introduces audiences to the French artisans and consultants, from cabinetmakers to food historians, that brought Coppola’s decadent vision to life. Of course, the exhibition would be incomplete without Milena Canonero’s Oscar-winning costumes and Manolo Blahnik’s dazzling heels, brought together from all corners of the world. These frothy confections, worn on mannequins bearing Dunst’s and Schwartzman’s uncanny visages, are complemented by Durham’s amusing candid film snaps, often picturing the cast’s behind-the-scenes antics, whether listening to music with headphones or taking a cigarette break. Ultimately Delalex believes no one at Versailles could have predicted that Coppola’s film “would have such a remarkable life.” “Its visual language continues to inspire interior design, photography, fashion, and even pastry,” said the curator, noting, perhaps, the movie’s greatest influence has been on Versailles itself. “For many people today, the Marie-Antoinette style has become synonymous with Sofia Coppola’s style — many visitors come here hoping to see the Versailles of the film. Her aesthetic is so strong, it’s like a work of art.” In the Bedchamber, a gossamer gown reflects Marie Antoinette’s stylistic shift towards more naturalistic attire at the end of the film Stephanie Sporn The Movable Mirrors Boudoir features a recreation of one of the film’s most iconic scenes in which the queen is surrounded by sweets Stephanie Sporn The Reception Room features mannequins engaging in the popular 18th-century pastimes that fueled some of the film’s most riotous scenes Stephanie Sporn Several display cases are dedicated to images and sample materials used to craft the queen’s Grand Chamber, reconstructed in a nearby château to exacting detail Stephanie Sporn Marie Antoinette’s (Kirsten Dunst) and Louis XVI’s (Jason Schwartzman) wedding ensembles are displayed in the Chapel Stephanie Sporn THR

title: ‘Imperfect Women’ Renewed For Season 2 By Apple Centered On Kerry Washington’s Character Eleanor
full_text: Skip to main content Dismiss News Banner Breaking News New Skydance Sets Top Executive Structure As Paramount-WBD Merger Set To Close Read the full story By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Imperfect Women’ Renewed For Season 2 By Apple Centered On Kerry Washington’s Character Eleanor James Van Der Beek Remembered In Tearful ‘Dawson’s Creek’ Reunion At Greg Berlanti’s Heroes Gala That Also Honored Katherine LaNasa Post-Merger Skydance Keeping Both HBO Max & Paramount+ Streaming Brands View All October 5, 2026 11:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Kerry Washington in 'Imperfect Women Apple TV+ Call it Imperfect Woman . The trend of streaming limited series becoming ongoing ones continues with Apple TV ordering a second season of thriller Imperfect Women . Taking a spinoff approach, it will follow one of the limited series’ three titular characters, Eleanor, played by Kerry Washington . Imperfect Women , based on Araminta Hall’s novel, revolved around best friends Eleanor and Mary (Elisabeth Moss) as they tried to solve the murder of the third member of their friends group, Nancy (Kate Mara), seen in flashbacks. Washington and Moss executive produced the original installment in addition to starring and will also both executive produce Season 2. Related Stories Casting Scott Foley Joins Apple TV's 'Shrinking' For Season 4 News All The Songs In 'Ted Lasso' Season 4 So Far There is no second Imperfect Women book so there is no source material for Season 2. Instead, it is based on an original story from series creator Annie Weisman and Justin Hillian. The two will serve as co-showrunners on the second season, which will change locations from Los Angeles, where Season 1 was set. Watch on Deadline In Season 2, Eleanor (Washington) returns to her hometown roots in the affluent black enclave of Martha’s Vineyard, only to find that beneath it’s idyllic surface, lie secrets and scandals that threaten to upend everything she thought she knew about her past.” For now, there are no plans for Moss’ Mary and Nancy’s widower Robert (Joel Kinnaman) to be in the second installment which picks up on the Eleanor’s flash-forward scene in the finale, which resonated with fans. It showed her moving away from the toxic dynamic of her relationships and enjoying a new life on a yacht with a new love interest. While cast deals are still being worked out, expected to return as part of the new Eleanor-centered installment are Leslie Odom Jr., who plays her brother, and Sheryl Lee Ralph, who plays their mother. As for the lingering question over Mary and Robert’s ambiguous glance at the end of the finale as the two were seen celebrating the birthday of Mary’s daughter together, that may be answered in Season 2 with a reference of the characters’ status. “We were thrilled to see how deeply these women and their stories resonated with audiences around the world, and I’m so excited to step back into Eleanor’s shoes,” Washington said. “She’s intelligent and strong, but she also finds herself navigating complicated and sometimes messy situations. We at Simpson Street along with our incredible partners at Apple and Love & Squalor Pictures can’t wait to explore a fresh chapter for her and share where this story takes us next.” The long list of limited series that have been picked up for additional installments include Apple TV’s Reasonable Doubt, Netflix’s Untamed, Squid Game, The Beast In Me and Beef , HBO’s Big Little Lies, The White Lotus, True Detective and Task , HBO’s Good American Family and FX’s Shōgun. Imperfect Women is a co-production between 20th Television and Apple Studios. The second season is created, co-showrun and executive produced by Weisman and Hillian, and executive produced by Washington for her Simpson Street banner alongside Pilar Savone. Moss and Lindsey McManus, who initially optioned the book, via their production company Love & Squalor Pictures are executive producers alongside author Hall. “After a wildly entertaining first season, driven by the performances of Kerry, Lizzie and Kate, we jumped at the opportunity to expand the world of Imperfect Women through Kerry’s fan favorite character of Eleanor,” said Matt Cherniss, Apple TV’s head of programming. “Annie and Justin’s thrilling new story felt like an exciting and natural next chapter. title: ‘Imperfect Women’ Renewed for Second Season at Apple TV
full_text: Skip to main content By Rick Porter Plus Icon Rick Porter Television Business Editor rickporter Follow Sign Up View All October 5, 2026 11:00am Kerry Washington in 'Imperfect Women' Apple TV Logo text Add another show to the ranks of no longer limited series: Apple TV ‘s Imperfect Women . The streamer has ordered a second season of the drama, with Kerry Washington set to reprise her role as Eleanor. Justin Hillian ( The Chi, Snowfall ) is also joining the series, based on a novel by Araminta Hall, as co-showrunner with series creator and season one showrunner Annie Weisman. The renewal for Imperfect Women comes about five months after the first season concluded. The show was initially positioned as a limited series, with Elisabeth Moss and Kate Mara starring alongside Washington. Moss, whose Love & Squalor Pictures optioned the novel, won’t reprise her on-screen role but remains an executive producer. title: ‘Tulsa King’ Renewed for Season 5, Moving to New York City
full_text: Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All October 5, 2026 11:00am Sylvester Stallone in 'Tulsa King.' Brian Douglas/Paramount+ Logo text Tulsa King is leaving Tulsa. Paramount+ has renewed the hit series for a fifth season, with a surprise twist — the production is moving to New York City. The story will bring Dwight “The General” Manfredi ( Sylvester Stallone ) back to his roots, with production now underway (previous seasons of the series have been shot in Atlanta and Oklahoma). The switch makes Tulsa King the first show from the famously heartland-focused Taylor Sheridan to film a season in New York or Los Angeles ( The Madison shot some scenes in Manhattan but was largely set in Montana). Related Stories TV Casey Bloys Indicates HBO Max and Paramount+ More Likely to Be Bundled Than Combined Movies Sylvester Stallone Reacts to Biopic 'I Play Rocky': "I'm Not Dead Yet. Aren't We Jumping the Gun?" “We are thrilled to bring fans even more of this incredible series and to be shooting the next season of Tulsa King in New York, where Dwight Manfredi’s story will continue to evolve,” said Drew Brown, executive vp, physical production, Paramount Television Studios. “We’re proud of the work we’ve done in Georgia, and it remains an important venue for us.” Empire State Development president, CEO and commissioner Hope Knight — an appointee of New York Governor Kathy Hochul — said in a statement: “We’re excited to welcome the cast and crew of Tulsa King to New York state for its fifth season. Under Governor Hochul’s leadership, New York has built an unmatched home for film and television — world-class talent, iconic locations and a film tax credit program that delivers real jobs and investment for New Yorkers. Tulsa King represents the latest in a growing list of projects proudly filmed in New York.” Hochul is up for reelection this year, and is facing off against Republican Bruce Blakeman. In addition, Tulsa King is adding several new cast members, and upping Stallone’s daughter, Scarlet Rose Stallone, to a series regular. Also joining the cast in series regular roles are Erik Palladino ( I Play Rocky ), Glenn Fleshler ( Billions ), Anthony Skordi ( The Last Frontier) and Nickola Shreli ( Power Book IV: Force ). Executive producer Terence Winter will continue to serve as head writer on the series, which has changed showrunners several times over the years. The news comes ahead of the season four premiere of Tulsa King on Oct. 16. In the new season, Dwight (Stallone) “fights to legitimize his empire and protect his crew as corrupt politicians, dangerous new enemies and a crushing personal loss hit from every direction. However, every hard-won gain comes with even harder truths: about loyalty, leadership and the cost of ambition. Each move drags Dwight deeper into the street instincts he left behind in New York — turning Tulsa into a battleground and Dwight into the one threat no one can afford to underestimate.” In addition to Stallone, Tulsa King stars Martin Starr, Jay Will, Vincent Piazza, Annabella Sciorra, Chris Caldovino, McKenna Quigley Harrington, Frank Grillo, Mike “Cash Flo” Walden, James Russo, Kevin Pollak, Neal McDonough, with Garrett Hedlund and Dana Delany. Gretchen Mol also joined the cast for season 4 as a series regular. THR

The Sylvester Stallone series has been renewed for a fifth season at Paramount+ as the production migrates from Georgia to the Big Apple, coinciding with the Season 5 storyline. The renewal comes ahead of the Season 4 premiere on Oct. 16. Stallone’s daughter Scarlet Rose Stallone, who has played Spencer on all four seasons of the show, has been promoted to series regular. Plus, four fresh faces are joining the cast in series regular roles: Erik Palladino (“I Play Rocky”), Glenn Fleshler (“Billions”), Anthony Skordi (“The Last Frontier”) and Nickola Shreli (“Power Book IV: Force”). title: I Was Humiliated, Spooned and Kissed on the Lips at L.A.’s Strangest Sold-Out Show
full_text: × Skip to main content By Seth Abramovitch Plus Icon Seth Abramovitch Senior Writer SethAbramovitch Follow Sign Up View All October 5, 2026 10:58am The Pineapple Show Candle House Collective Candle House Collective The Pineapple nearly lost me before I got through the door. My instructions via text message were to meet at an abandoned alley in North Hollywood at precisely 8:40 p.m. I was told, rather ominously, not to “talk to anyone outside” and to knock on the black door under a State Farm sign. What the instructions neglected to mention was that there were two State Farm signs in the alley. I knocked on the door beneath the first one I spotted. Nothing. With my appointed time approaching, I texted the number I’d been given. A response came quickly: Wrong State Farm sign. The correct door was about 50 feet down. Related Stories Lifestyle Neil Patrick Harris, Julianne Hough, Austin Scott to Return to Broadway in 'Damn Yankees' Lifestyle Phylicia Rashad Tapped to Direct Adaptation of August Wilson's 'Fences' at Mark Taper Forum I made it. But the disorientation turned out to be an appropriate introduction to The Pineapple . When the door finally opened, an agitated young man who resembled Ryan Gosling (Rett Keeter) shined an LED flashlight directly into my eyes, a gesture that would become familiar over the next hour. “Do you know the safe word?” he demanded. I did. He instructed me to shout, “I want to find aliens!” I complied. Louder. “I WANT TO FIND ALIENS!” Louder. “I WANT TO FIND ALIENS!!!” At some point, he noticed something else. “Do you laugh when you’re nervous?” Apparently I had been laughing quite a bit. The answer was yes. I was nervous. But laughter was also a way of maintaining some distance from what was happening, remaining the amused observer rather than the person to whom this was actually happening. He seemed determined to take that away from me. And that’s about as much as I’m going to tell you about what happens next. Part of the pleasure of The Pineapple is not knowing what is waiting on the other side of a door, down a darkened passageway or sometimes inches from your face. Over the course of a remarkably packed 60 minutes, I crawled, squeezed and stumbled through a succession of spaces and encounters that could be funny, frightening, ridiculous and unexpectedly intimate. At various points I thought of Bugonia , Barbarian and the kitchen sequence in The Backrooms . But those comparisons only get you so far. Unlike a movie, The Pineapple doesn’t let you sit safely outside the frame: You are the thing being acted upon. The privilege doesn’t come cheap: Tickets run about $250. But there appears to be a hungry audience for this kind of hyper-experiential entertainment. The initial run of roughly 80 performances sold out almost instantly. Some explanation of the people responsible for all this is probably in order. Candle House Collective was founded in 2018 by Evan Neiden, who began experimenting with a peculiar form of immersive theater that didn’t necessarily require a theater at all. Its early productions infiltrated participants’ lives through phone calls, texts and emails. The idea was to collapse the distance between fiction and reality until, ideally, you stopped behaving like an audience member and simply reacted. That approach produced Claws , a one-person telephone thriller in which a frightened stranger calls asking for help with something lurking in his closet; and Lennox Mutual , an ongoing interactive epic disguised as a customer-service line for a mysterious “life en-surance” company. Candle House calls what it does “alternate reality theatre.” The conceit sounds gimmicky until you encounter what its performers can do with it. Writing about Claws and Lennox Mutual in The New Yorker , a critic described one of these encounters becoming “suddenly, uncannily real.” That’s the trick, and the performers in The Pineapple , conceived, designed, and directed by Neiden, are remarkably good at it. The difference is that this time Candle House has gotten out of your phone and into the room with you. There is nowhere for an actor to hide when his audience consists of a single stranger standing inches away. The talented performers — besides the intense Keeter, the cast includes Ian Michaels, Cece Kelly and Neiden himself — commit so completely to the reality of The Pineapple that, despite knowing perfectly well I’d bought a ticket to a theatrical experience in North Hollywood, there were moments when that knowledge became surprisingly difficult to access. They are also performing a second, largely invisible task: reading you. How frightened are you? How game are you? How far can this particular person be pushed? My nervous laughter wasn’t in a script. It was something the first actor noticed, understood and used. Over the course of the hour, the power relationships keep shifting. The participant who arrives determined to observe eventually discovers that observation isn’t really an option. The Pineapple does push, although not always in the ways you expect. At one point, a performer asked whether I had ever forgiven someone. Who? What had they done? Why had I forgiven them? By then, The Pineapple had trained me to answer questions rather than stand outside them analyzing why they were being asked. So I told him, not entirely sure why I was relaying such sensitive information. I revealed something deeply personal to a stranger inside this absurd fictional world, and then the show moved on. Except it hadn’t. Much later, what I’d told him came back to me, incorporated into the performance in a way I won’t reveal. It fucked with my head a little. It was also weirdly touching. The waiver I’d signed beforehand warned of physical contact, but that phrase doesn’t quite prepare you for what follows. I was touched, caressed, held and, at one point, kissed on the mouth. I found myself wondering whether I was experiencing those encounters differently than another audience member might. Would the audience member’s sexuality affect the experience, turning it from something exhilarating into something threatening? At what point does the identity of the person being touched become part of the work? Then another question occurred to me: What about the person doing the touching? For all the apparent power the performers exercise over you, this is also their job. They are being asked to enter unusually intimate physical situations with a succession of strangers. After the performance, I asked Neiden about the actors’ side of this peculiar bargain. Audience members are given a safeword, which stops the action. But Neiden told me the performers have exactly the same right. They can say it, too. (No one on either side of the equation has used it in L.A., while an earlier incarnation of The Pineapple in New Jersey resulted in a lone participant ending the experience.) That detail changed the way I thought about the preceding hour. The Pineapple is built around the sensation that control has been taken away from you. In reality, the whole elaborate illusion depends upon everyone in the room retaining the power to stop it. Which may be why the experience can go as far as it does. There is humiliation here, claustrophobia, physical vulnerability and an intimacy that occasionally brushes against the erotic. But there is also absurdity and a surprising amount of humor. The production keeps scrambling the emotional signals. Something threatening becomes funny, someone powerful becomes vulnerable, a ridiculous situation begins to feel alarmingly real. An hour after I’d knocked on the wrong door, I stumbled back onto the street, disoriented, a lei around my neck and wondering what the hell I had just experienced. A man was standing beside a parked Tesla. He looked at me and gave a slight, knowing smirk. For a moment, I wondered if he was part of The Pineapple , too. By then, I wasn’t entirely sure where the show ended. “Are you next?” I asked. He was. “How was it?” he asked. I looked at him. My first instinct was to assess who he was, what he might make of everything I’d just experienced. I couldn’t really tell. “I loved it,” I said, entirely unsure he’d feel the same way. THR

title: Iberseries Takeaways: Woody Allen on His New Film, Los Javis Pact With HBO Max, the Tales of Cachou the Brown Bear and More
full_text: Oct 5, 2026 10:54am PT Iberseries Takeaways: Woody Allen on His New Film, Los Javis Pact With HBO Max, the Tales of Cachou the Brown Bear and More More: Erik Barmack on AI; Banijay’s secret, Amazon MGM’s new action breed and the Holy Grail search for original crime By John Hopewell Plus Icon John Hopewell Chief International Correspondent john_hopewell Latest La Oreja de Van Gogh Songs Set to Power an Ambitious Romantic Musical From Fernando González Molina (EXCLUSIVE) 11 hours ago HBO Max Unveils Javier Calvo, Javier Ambrossi Drama Series, Created by ‘Anatomy’ Writer Fran Araújo and ‘Querer’ Scribe Eduard Sola (EXCLUSIVE) 5 days ago Mubi Takes Global on Los Javis ‘La Mesías’ and Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s ‘Riot Police’ as Movistar Plus Rolls Out Iconic Hits Around the World (EXCLUSIVE) 5 days ago See All Woody Allen in Madrid. Oct. 1, 2026 presenting his new film. Credit: Anna Marie de la Fuente When the going gets tough, the tough get going to places like Iberseries & Platino Industria. Its 6th edition, also a pre-Mipcom warm-up, ran over Sept.29-Oct. 2 at Madrid’s Matadero, its rehabilitated orange-red brick former slaughterhouse. That setting seems appropriate. There’s little evidence that Ampere Analysis’ maxim, coined a couple of years ago – a contracting sector chasing a 75% of peak TV business – has not changed. Related Stories 'Voices' Review: Singing Through Fear and Anxiety in a Detroit-Set Musical Thriller ‘Evil Genius’ Review: Courteney Cox Fashions the Pizza Bomber Case Into a Broad, Shrilly Played Farce Some parts of the TV business have hardly altered at all, such as its dependence on great writing, Steve Matthews, Banijay head of scripted, creative, said at an Iberseries company Spotlight. Popular on Variety Yet most companies, from Super Indies and network giants to small former auteur producers are pushing into AI, if only for backroom operations, and microdramas to push back against spiralling costs and diminishing revenues, sustaining cash-flow and not losing out on new growth opportunities. That in turn is driving new mindsets. Making microdramas has made Argentinean producer Lorena Quevedo think of how long certain proceses take in cinema and series. “Suddenly a series we thought had an impossible budget we took up again saying: ‘If we made this microdrama, we cannot not make this series.’” Needful of such insights, delegates broke attendance records up a massive 20% to 3,400 including day passes. Iberseries & Platino Industria is organized by rights collection society EGEDA and Foundation Secuoya, in collaboration with producers’ assn. Fipca and sponsorship from Madrid Film Office and Film Madrid Region. 10 takeaways: Woody Allen The big star at Iberseries, or nearby at least in another part of Madrid, was the 90 year-old New Yorker. Starring an ensemble cast of Marton Csokas, Jemima Kirke Jakob Oftebro, Peter Vives and Alexi Wasser, the provisionally entitled Woody Allen Fall Project rolls Oct. 5 with WestEnd Films handling world sales. Small and debonair, Allen didn’t reveal so much about his upcoming film at an Oct. 1 press conference – he rarely does – though he teased it was a “comedy with romance, intrigue and infidelity.” He also said that Madrid – elegant and beautiful – was perfect for the “diplomatic atmosphere” he wanted for the film. The jury is out how the film will go. “It has to live up to my expectations. That doesn’t mean that it will, but I’ll do my best,” he said. Allen has however made pointed use of seeming postcard settings before, as in “Vicky Cristina Barcelona,” one of his most successful international shoots. Los Javis , Mubi and an HBO Max Coup In one of the biggest news announcements at Iberseries, Mubi acquired global on drama series “La Mesías,” created by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi and sold by Movistar Plus International, which is to TV is what “La Bola Negra” is to cinema. In another, and a coup for HBO Max unveiled development on an enticing new crime series, to be exec produced by Los Javis at their Madrid manner Suma Content. The series is created by Fran Araújo, who co-penned Intl. Emmy-nominated “The Anatomy of the Moment,” and “Querer” co-scribe Eduard Sola, two of Spain’s most exciting writing talents. Most all talk about the Javis’ turns on “La Bola Negra.” They – and indeed HBO Max – are also rapidly creating ever more powerful creative hubs. (L-R) Fran Araújo, Edu Sola (L-R) Fran Araujo, Eduard Sola Credit: Patricia J Garcinuno Erik Barmack on What He Got Wrong About AI, and What He Might Have Got Right, to the Horror of Some Iberseries debated genre.The real horror story for many was AI. Just take the macro stats. Barmack delivered some stats. Revenues for just two U.S. AI companies, Anthropic and OpenAI, are projected to grow to an annual $700 million in the next couple of years, worth 13-15 times the value of Europe and Latin America’s entire media industries. AI is “much more disruptive” than sound, cable TV or streaming. And if “AI companies don’t continue to grow, the entire stock market will crash.” Barmack is a highly respected former Netflix international head. He’s also a recognised AI expert. Could he be wrong? To the relief of much of his producer audience, he did say he’s been wrong on one count. When Sora started, I was sort of convinced that it was over and that we’d be stuck on these loops of of watching 15-second generated clips targeted to your algorithm. That turned out to be wrong because it was too expensive, basically, to make these videos. And there wasn’t a big enough audience for what’s called AI slop.” The Holy Grail: Original Crime and Cachou Presented at Iberseries, the big new Movistar Plus-Arte series “Killing a Bear” is a murder mystery, where the victim is Cachou. A giant Pyrenean brown bear, his death in real life and on screen sparks a criminal investigation, as the event is recounted episode by episode by different characters in six radically warring versions. This originality builds as it feeds into a broader portrait lending historical depth of an ancient Spain battling environmentalists and E.U. regulation to preserve its way of life. Crime still pays, accounting for 27% of scripted TV orders and 24% of first-run scripted TV ordered globally, making it the single most commissioned TV genre, Ampere Analysis’ Guy Bisson tells Variety . But what operators and big indies want is original crime to cut through the crowd, one of the sector’s Holy Grails. Eduard Fernández in ‘Killing a Bear’ Bárbara Sánchez Palomero Banijay’s Secret Mipcom’s conference will kick off with a Jeff Zucker-Marco Bassetti keynote, moderated by Variety co-Editor in Chief Cynthia Littelton, post the Banijay-All3Media $8 billion merger. What’s Banijay’s secret? One obviously is scalable franchises. Another is its network of 170 companies worldwide. “All of these are based on creativity, based on talent, based on writing,” Steve Matthews, Banijay head of scripted, creative, said at an Iberseries Banijay Spotlight. Connecting with great talent, and giving them the trust and resources to make the titles they envision is indeed the key to some of the greatest production operations and producers in the world. Microdramas Open Up Inevitably, Iberseries hosted a vertical drama panel. “I’m from Team Melodrama,” said Argentinean producer Lorena Quevedo, a panelist, arguing the key was “romantic tension.” Her first microdrama – and indeed Argentina’s, – “Dinero, Armas y Feliz Navidad,” released on ReelShort in September 2025, hit 273 million views. Most microdramas are classic melodramas,. The format, however, is opening up in the Spanish-speaking world. Though its slate is primarily made up of vertical dramas, Telemundo Studios has begun to develop 20-episode 10-minute horizontal series, said Telemundo’s Clo Fernandez. 3Pas Studios has recently made a vertical musical, is considering a comedic microdrama, added Javier Williams. Quevedo has produced a vertical actioner. One Direction Amazon MGM is Heading In International: Genre at Scale An Amazon MGM Studios Spotlight was led by Javiera Balmaceda, head of international originals, Latin America, Canada and Australia, and Nicole Morganti, Prime Video head of international originals, Italy & Southern Europe. Both pointed to big action swings – Mexico’s “Venganza,” produced by El Estudio’s Pablo Cruz, and espionage actioner Zeta,” starring Mario Casas as one way to go. Both topped Prime Video Global Top 10 charts. Latin America’s challenge, Balmaceda noted is not necessarily a lack of talent, but a shortage of experience and opportunities to work at scale. Spanish Cinema: Size Matters Scale threaded various panels. Another Example Spain made 423 feature films in 2025, according to the European Audiovisual Observatory. In 2026, as Iberseries unspooled, only four movies can be described as box office hits: “Torrente for President” (€29.1 million: $32.8 million), “Tadeo and the Magic Lamp,” (€7.2 million) “Aida y vuelta” (€5.1 million), “La Bola Negra” (€14.9 million and counting fast) and The Beloved. All are high-end for Spain. Three are based on huge Spanish IP. Another stars Javier Bardem. “The future of Spanish cinema does not lie in making more films, but in getting more people to want to see them,” Atresmedia Cine MD Jaime de Ortiz de Artiñano said late August. That sentiment ran through multiple panels at Iberseries. IPs: Their Power Only 12-14% of new series premieres each year are based on existing IP but existing IP accounts for 40%-50% of the top 100 most in-demand series, Parrot Analytics Jaime Otero said at Iberseries. On average, titles based on IP has 2.3 times more demand than original titles. That rises to 2.9 times titles inspired by real events and 3 times for literary adaptations. Multiples companies are putting large faith in big IPs. At Iberseries, for example, Luis Fernandez, Telemundo president, drilled down at a keynote on its ways forward. One is live events. Another reaching out to YA auds. And another, a 2027 schedule which includes new seasons of “La Reina del Sur,” El Señor de los Cielos” and “Sin Senos No Hay Paraíso,” an awesome franchise trifecta. Spanish-Language New Markets Spanish-language series are successful because they have a captive audience of 600 million native Spanish speakers. Their growth, however, lies elsewhere, Parrot Analytics’ Jaime Otero suggested at Iberseries opening panel. The global demand for series from Spain, Portugal and Latin America series has increased 25% since late August 2024., driven by countries outside the region such as South Korea, up 245%, Japan and China, up 119% in two years, or in Scandinavia where it has doubled. Meanwhile demand in Latin America has edged up or down, according to the territory. Little wonder then that Spanish export and trade board ICEX held an event to boost Spanish talent in Shanghai this July. And a Bake’s Dozen of Deals Announced by Variety at This Year’s Iberseries & Platino Industria: *Movistar Plus International unveiled 33 new sales deals, led by Mubí taking the world on “La Mesias,” and to “Riot Police,” from “The Beloved” director Rodrigo Sorogoyen. International distribution deals were also led by ‘The Anatomy of a Moment,” “Querer,” “The New Years” and ‘The Nameless.’ *HBO Max announced that “La Bola Negra” writer-director-producers Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi are set to exec produce an ambitious new HBO Max drama series created by Fran Araújo and Eduard Sola. *Beta Film has unveiled broad international sales for “Rex – Vienna Calling,” the latest incarnation of the hugely popular three-decade-old “Rex – A Cop’s Best Friend” franchise, as production gets underway on a second season. *Globoplay has greenlit an adaptation of Raphael Montes’ “Uma Mulher no Escuro,” from Banijay Entertainment’s A Fábrica Brazilian banner. The order was announced at an Iberseries Banijay Spotlight panel. *‘Elite’ star Ester Expósito is circling ‘Stink Eye,’ an Iberseries Co-Production & Financing Forum Title. * “The Good Girls” lead Ilse Salas is set to to star in Quijote Films’ “To Die on Your Feet” (“Morir de Pie”) another project pitched at Iberseries & Platino Industria Forum. *”Sin Filtro’ producer JK Media is producing its first original microdramas shot in the U.S. for TelevisaUnivision’s ViXMicrO. *Belgian royalty series “King of Hearts” has secured key VRT backing. The coming-of-age drama series is from Giles Coulier, whose company, De Wereldvrede, is behind such hits as 2019 series “War of the Worlds” and Prix Europa winner, “Albatros.” *‘Plaza Catedral’ director Abner Benaim, Chile’s Daniela Vega and Alfredo Castro have boarded fiction series “School of the Americas.” *France’s Halley Production has boarded thriller ‘Carro Seco,’ about a killer who targets unscrupulous Barcelona real estate speculators. Javier Polo directs the buzz project at Iberseries & Platino Industria’s Co-Production and Financing Forum. *Chile’s Sanfic is set to screen late documentarian Antonio Caro’s swan song “Monguen” among nine Chilean pics in Competition. *”Strawberry and Chocolate” star Jorge Perugorría and Brazil’s Thiago Lacerda lead Havana-Set “Hotel Nacional,” another Iberseries Forum project. title: Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Bumps ‘Choosin’ Texas’ Out of No. 1 on Hot 100; ‘Encore’ Tracks Fill Four Out of Five Top Slots
full_text: Oct 5, 2026 10:34am PT Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Bumps ‘Choosin’ Texas’ Out of No. 1 on Hot 100; ‘Encore’ Tracks Fill Four Out of Five Top Slots By Chris Willman Plus Icon Chris Willman Senior Music Writer and Chief Music Critic ChrisWillman Latest Taylor Swift’s ‘Patient Zero’ Bumps ‘Choosin’ Texas’ Out of No. 1 on Hot 100; ‘Encore’ Tracks Fill Four Out of Five Top Slots 31 minutes ago CMA’s ‘Celebration of Dolly Parton’ Special Slates 20 Performers, Including Ella Langley, Lainey Wilson, Molly Tuttle and Reba McEntire 2 hours ago Is ‘Rubber Soul’ the Beatles’ Best Album? The Answer to That is as Malleable as the Shifting Track Lists, but This ‘Super Deluxe’ Is Super Essential: Boxed Set Review 19 hours ago See All Michael Buckner At least for one week, America finally chose differently when it came to the nation’s most consumed song. Ella Langley’s “Choosin’ Texas” took a breather from its record-breaking run atop the Billboard Hot 100 to make room for Taylor Swift ‘s “ Patient Zero ,” which claims the No. 1 spot in its first week out, to no one’s surprise. Swift released four new tracks going into the chart week, all part of her “ The Life of a Showgirl: The Encore ” project, and all of them bowed in the uppermost rans of the Hot 100. Following the Langley song, which fell just one slot to No. 2, Swift owns the next three positions, with “Cleveland!,” “Babylon” and “Pink Clouding” landing at Nos. 3, 4 and 5, respectively. Related Stories 'What Remains' Review: A Pensive but Stirring Drama Finds Poetry in the Landscapes of Rural Turkey ‘Anchors Aweigh’ Review: A Cynical Comedian Reflects on His Youth in an Abridged Mockumentary “Patient Zero” becomes her 16th No. 1 song on the chart, and puts her a little closer to overtaking the only two artists who can claim more, the Beatles with 20 and Mariah Carey with 19. Popular on Variety Billboard reported that she has also tied a record with this No. 1 bow. With this, she has 10 songs that have debuted at No. 1, a figure she now shares with the former solo record-holder, Drake. News of Swift topping the Hot 100 comes one day after it was reported that “The Life of a Showgirl” returned to the No. 1 position on the Billboard 200 album chart for the first time since January. That album now has 13 cumulative weeks in the top position there. (Billboard and Luminate count all versions of the album — the original and the newly expanded “Encore” edition — as one.) The rest of the Hot 100’s top 10 is rounded out by Stella Lefty’s “Boston” at No. 6, Morgan Wallen’s “Been by Now” at No. 7, Ariana Grande’s “Hate That I Made You Love Me” at No. 8, Olivia Rodrigo’s “Stupid Song” at No. 9 and Tame Impala and Jennie’s “Dracula” at No. 10. Swift stands a strong chance at having a second week at No. 1. Bolstering that likelihood: Fans who preordered physical copies of “Patient Zero” just got a notice that their singles are shipping this week, which means those sales will count in the song’s second charting week. For chart watchers wondering whether Ella Langley can hold on to her record for the song with the most weeks at No. 1, versus relinquishing it back to Mariah Carey, the coming weeks hold some suspense, as to how “Patient Zero” might affect that. Carey’s “All I Want for Christmas Is You” is highly likely to reascend to No. 1 for a couple of weeks or more during the month of December, as it usually does, so it could overtake “Choosin’ Texas”… unless Langley is able to get some more insurance weeks in at the top of the chart between Swift’s song falling off and Carey’s coming back up. title: David Berson to Take Over Combined Sports Operations at Skydance, Luis Silberwasser to Exit

Discovery., and that company’s top sports executive, Luis Silberwasser , will exit. “I have tremendous respect for our leadership and for the leaders of CBS Sports, who are great colleagues and friends. I believe in the strategy ahead and, above all, in the people who will carry this work forward,” Silberwasser said in a memo to staffers Monday “The success of this organization has always been about the talent, commitment and character of its people, and I know those qualities will continue to define it in the years ahead.” Related Stories Kim Kardashian Taps Olympians Chloe Kim, Jutta Leerdam and More for New NikeSKIMS Campaign Berson will take the reins of a merged portfolio that includes not only CBS Sports’ NFL and Masters golf rights, but a Warner package that includes NHL and Major League Baseball games along with the U.S. rights to the French Open. title: Joey and Matthew Lawrence on Launching Their New Graphic Novel, ’90s Nostalgia and Hopes for an Animated Series
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kimberly Nordyke Plus Icon Kimberly Nordyke Managing Editor, Digital View All October 5, 2026 10:33am From left: Matthew, Joey and Andrew Lawrence. Derek Brajevich The Lawrence Brothers are embarking on a new adventure as detectives — at least, in the comics. Last summer, Joey, Matt and Andrew Lawrence announced that they were teaming with the Berkowitz Brothers, Sean Von Gorman and Z2 for The Lawrence Brothers Detective Agency, an original graphic novel series. They made their announcement via a Kickstarter campaign that allowed fans to be part of the project from the start, as well as appearances at San Diego Comic-Con. The fruits of their effort is now available for purchase online and in stores (a deluxe edition featuring an exclusive retro Trapper Keeper-style slipcase is available for purchase at Z2’s website ). The story reimagines the former child stars as reluctant heroes battling a conspiracy that’s warping the very fabric of fame. The tale, set against the surreal backdrop of a corrupted Hollywood, follows the brothers as they survive a monster outbreak at a fan con, among other adventures. It’s describes as “a satirical fever dream about identity, memory and the absurdity of pop culture. Think BoJack Horsema n meets Chinatown . Smart, surreal, and completely not what anyone expected … and that’s exactly the point.” Related Stories Beyond the Book Inside the 'Verity' Adaptation: Crafting a Mystery Where Nothing Is Certain Beyond the Book Zoe Kazan on Honoring Steinbeck's 'East of Eden' for Netflix Series While Rethinking Its Characters The brothers were heavily involved in the creation of graphic novel, which they co-created and wrote with the Berkowitz Brothers (Josh Gad’s The Write r), a production company founded by Ben and Max Berkowitz that creates and develops original comic book IP as a direct pipeline for film and television. Additional writing for the graphic novel came from Brian Yuran, with art by Eisner-nominated Sean Von Gorman ( Toe Tag Riot, Pawn Shop ) of Comics. Z2 is comic book and graphic novel publisher that woks with closely top artists and musicians. The darkly funny, satirical graphic novel pokes fun at their past as child stars; their collective credits include such TV shows and movies as Gimme a Break!, Blossom, Mrs. Doubtfire, Boy Meets World and their own sitcom, Brotherly Love. (More recently, the trio reunited onscreen for the indie holiday film Mistletoe Mixup and a sequel. In addition, they co-host the Brotherly Love Podcast, which features confessions, behind-the-scenes stories and their takes on growing up famous. Joey and Matthew also joined other ’90s icons recently for HGTV’s renovation competition Totally ’90s House. ) “We made [the graphic novel] for the for the fans and the community that supported us for 45 years, so hopefully you guys [the fans] will enjoy it,” Joey Lawrence tells The Hollywood Reporter. “That’s what it was intended to be: absolute pure enjoyment. Hopefully, you’ll laugh and you’ll reminisce a little bit, and then hopefully you’ll want to come back for more. That’s what it really is; there’s nothing more complicated than that.” Joey and Matthew Lawrence recently talked to THR about their new graphic novel, the current wave of ’90s nostalgia and their hopes for an animated series. How did the idea for the graphic novel come about? MATTHEW LAWRENCE We’ve always loved the format because you can have so much fun with it. We used to do these family vacations every year, and one summer family vacation, probably 15-20 years ago, we were coming up with these storylines. Somebody had lost something on the beach, and we were like, what if the Lawrence brothers formed a detective agency? We were just joking around. We came up with all these plot twists, and we thought, this would be a great graphic novel or animated series. Honestly, it’s always been in the back of our minds since then. Then, we were … introduced to the Berkowitz Brothers. They were like, hey, do you have any interest in doing one of these? And we said, well, actually we’ve thought about doing this for a long time. And, of course, they’re brothers, we’re brothers, so it just kind of made sense, and this is the product that came out of that. JOEY LAWRENCE We were all big fans of Scooby-Doo and the Hardy Boys, and we thought, man, it’d be so cool if we could sort of do like an origin story, sort of an adult Scooby-Doo, because there’s nothing like that out there. And that’s why we have the van. Honestly, it’s an ’80s van, it’s the A-team van, but with Scooby-Doo colors. (Laughs ) MATTHEW LAWRENCE We blend a lot of different genres. JOEY LAWRENCE Obviously, our way in was through nostalgia and the era with slime and Gak, making fun of ourselves and self-deprecation. If we get a chance to do more of these, it will be standalone cases like Scooby-Doo and ideally an animated series — that’s what we want to do. And like Matt was saying, the art form, the genre is so expansive and very forgiving in terms of what we can get away with, and that’s always fun. MATTHEW LAWRENCE Literally, if you can dream it and draw it, you can make it happen. As you mentioned , you do poke fun at yourselves, which was really fun to see. Was that hard to do, or do you generally have a sense of humor about all of this? MATTHEW LAWRENCE That’s how we face everything, including tragedy and sad moments in our lives. We always try to find levity in most situations, and most of the time, yes, we’re very self-deprecating. We get it. We want people to know that we’re part of the joke as well. JOEY LAWRENCE If you can’t have fun with yourself and make fun of yourself, honestly, I feel like — you’ve just got to get over yourself. How much of your actual personalities is in these characters? Is it all you, or is it an exaggerated part of you? MATTHEW LAWRENCE Whether you’re an actor or you’re a voice-over actor, I think you always put a shred of yourself in everything, right? And then you take dramatic license, and we have some fun. I feel like basic principles, like the birth-order thing, like I definitely play the middle, Joey’s the older, the leader. But they’re really exaggerated. And I’ve got a chameleon [as he also does in the graphic novel]; I’m a big, reptile guy — that kind of stuff. JOEY LAWRENCE It’s real and then we expand upon it and make it nuts. But the dynamic is real. Can you talk about the process of coming up with the storyline? How hands-on were you? JOEY LAWRENCE We knew the world we wanted to put it in. Obviously we had never written a graphic novel, so we relied on, like Matt was saying, the Berkowitz Brothers to help us out with that, and they really crafted it into the story. But we were back-and-forth every step of the way, and we thought it would be fun to do sort of a Hollywood story, not in Hollywood necessarily, right? So we set it at this con, which is Hollywood-adjacent, and then somebody’s kidnapping these lost ’90s stars. MATTHEW LAWRENCE And by the way, there’s kind of a deep metaphor there as well, especially when you see a lot of child actors really face a lot of turmoil in their lives, and especially from the generation that we were in. A lot of the people that we came up with aren’t around anymore. So there’s this deepness to it that we then just kind of put all this real fun craziness around, but there’s a current, like the lost ’90s stars, child stars, there’s a current there that we wanted to have a little bit of a deeper meaning. And the ’90s is back in a big way. What do you attribute to that coming back, and how do you feel being part of that revival? JOEY LAWRENCE I think people are really craving a little more analog world. I think they’re craving a little bit more of how things used to be. I think there’s a lot of buyer’s remorse is this sort of new-age technology, everybody being downloaded every five seconds onto something new with a new password, a new code, a new update. I think it’s just an anxiety-ridden time, and I feel like people are really going, man, I miss the days of riding my bike and shooting some hoops and gathering around a TV to watch something or making a mix tape or a mix CD. MATTHEW LAWRENCE You were actually having family dinners that weren’t technology. And you had to talk and enjoy each other. JOEY LAWRENCE I really hope we find a balance. Obviously, this technology world has been thrust upon us and we’ve become frenzied with it. But I’m hoping that like a pendulum, it’s so heavy, and I feel now we’re sort of going, wait a minute, put a couple of rocks back on this side of the scale and maybe we’ll find a balance. I really hope we do. I feel like we kind of had the perfect balance in the late ’90s, to be honest with you. We could text, we had our phones, we had internet, we had cable. But yet we weren’t consumed by the technology. So I feel like that is probably why people are really craving that old-school world. Were you all big graphic-novel fans growing up? JOEY LAWRENCE We were always comic book fans. We loved the comic book world. Andy was nuts [about it]. MATTHEW LAWRENCE Andy actually introduced me to all this stuff. JOEY LAWRENCE Andy collected everything he could, like original Superman comics. MATTHEW LAWRENCE He was a big comic book guy, and this is the one moment where I really wish he was sitting here right now because he would go into his whole collection. [Andrew was busy with a work commitment and couldn’t be present for the interview.] JOEY LAWRENCE We love the world. We think it’s so much fun. The original Scooby-Doo is an incredible graphic novel. I feel that entertainment used to be much more just entertainment, and not so much real realism. The balance there is out of whack too, in my opinion. It’s mostly realism and very little entertainment. People crave fun, escapism type of entertainment. MATTHEW LAWRENCE I’ve been really impressed with the younger generation. I thought it was we were lost totally, but the younger generation has been pushing back. They want more analog. They’ve been going to the malls. Now that they’ve discovered the ’90s, they’re like, yeah, I don’t want AI. I’m kind of hopeful that maybe the kids have got us covered. With your graphic novel, how much input did you have in the artwork and the drawings of yourselves and how each of you looks in graphic-novel form? MATTHEW LAWRENCE We were very involved with the artwork, the color coding, the way things looked, the individual looks of us — JOEY LAWRENCE — the way my back muscles look in that one picture. (Laughs) MATTHEW LAWRENCE And the chameleon I had. I was very specific. That’s one of my favorite pages — you flip the page and there’s just a spotlight on a little chameleon. I love that part. We were very involved, and [illustrator] Sean Von Gorman was awesome. Is it surreal to see yourself in comic-book form? JOEY LAWRENCE It is. We were in San Diego last year. We had a big panel to sort of launch the Kickstarter for the book, and it was [surreal]. MATTHEW LAWRENCE And really cool. You mentioned wanting to turn this into possibly an animated series. MATTHEW LAWRENCE That’d be awesome, especially if we could have a new generation discover this. JOEY LAWRENCE The Hardy Boys, grown-up Scooby-Doo. That’s what this would be, and it’d be so much fun to do it in the animated space. And voiced by you all, I presume? JOEY LAWRENCE Absolutely. Nobody can do this voice, man. (Laughs) You also have a podcast that you do with Andrew. Can you talk about that experience? MATTHEW LAWRENCE It’s like this little thing we never expected. We do it in our basement. It’s really homegrown; we don’t run ads. It’s just us. We get to reach people, and the response from the fans when we — whether we’re just having fun and talking, they get to feel like it reminds them of their family or that we brought up an issue that really helped them. It also it brings us closer every week. We got to sit down whether we like it or not. Most of the time he doesn’t like it. (Laughs) JOEY LAWRENCE I have to drive here. I have to schlep. (Laughs) MATTHEW LAWRENCE It’s in my basement, so I’m lucky. I just get to wake up, put on a T-shirt, and roll down. (Laughs) JOEY LAWRENCE Not me, I get all four children ready and I come here, you know. (Laughs) No, it’s great. It’s like the little engine that could. It just keeps growing and never would I thought that almost four years ago, that we would be still doing this. THR

title: Jasmine Curtis-Smith, Yao, Jamie Chung to Star in Rom-Com ‘We Could Be in Love’ (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All October 5, 2026 10:32am yao, Jasmine Curtis-Smith and Marie Jamora Thomas Brunot; Josh Tolentino; Bianca Catbangan Love might be in the air with a forthcoming romantic-comedy indie film . Production has begun on filmmaker Marie Jamora’s We Could Be in Love , The Hollywood Reporter has learned. Jasmine Curtis-Smith ( The Time That Remains ), yao ( Sinners ), Jamie Chung ( Copperhead ), Lou Diamond Phillips ( Gangland ), Tamlyn Tomita ( Karate Kid Part II ) and Airline Inthyrath (aka RuPaul’s Drag Race alum Jujubee) round out the cast for the feature that starts shooting next month on location in New York and Manila, Philippines . We Could Be in Love centers on Jasmine Aquino (Curtis-Smith), a working-class Filipina American woman who falls for Ambrose Lee (yao), the affluent heir to a Chinese-Filipino dynasty. Their burgeoning relationship leads to challenges involving class divides and deep-seated prejudices. Related Stories Movies David Cross, Thomas Mann, Hasan Minhaj's Comedy 'Lucy Schulman' From Ellie Sachs Lands Release (Exclusive) Movies Biopic About Gambling Influencer Vegas Matt in the Works From Filmmaker Mike Young (Exclusive) Jamora, a Filipina director who grew up in Manila, helms the film from a script by Terence Chen ( Meet Cute in Manhattan ). Producers include Geri Leigh Tiu and Sonca Nguyen for Tiger & Dog Production, alongside Annie Huang. Chen, Thea Jacinto Ugarte and Jon-Adrian “JJ” Velazquez are executive producing. Hannah Kittell is the costume designer, while Dino-Ray Ramos serves as cultural consultant. “I grew up in the Philippines watching all the Hollywood rom-coms with my mom,” says director Jamora, who has helmed episodes of Queen Sugar and Matlock and is attached to the thriller feature Imprint . “Now that I have the opportunity to direct an Asian-led romantic comedy outside the traditional American studio system, it’s so exciting to lean into the cultural nuance, authenticity and heart that global audiences are craving. Jasmine and yao bring a special combination of warmth, depth and chemistry to their characters. I cannot wait to share our film with the world.” Adds writer and executive producer Chen, “At its core, We Could Be In Love is a classic, swoon-worthy romance that doesn’t shy away from the real cultural and economic friction points within our communities. We are thrilled to be filming in New York and Manila and capturing the vibrant, modern backdrop of these cities.” THR

title: ‘Verity’ Star Anne Hathaway on Whether She’s Team Letter or Team Manuscript
full_text: × Skip to main content By Beatrice Verhoeven Plus Icon Beatrice Verhoeven Awards Editor bverhoeven Follow Sign Up View All October 5, 2026 10:30am Everett [Warning: This story contains spoilers for the Verity film]. The ending of Verity has fans divided: Did Verity Crawford tell the truth in her manuscript, or was the letter Lowen found at the end of the movie telling the true story? Like fans of the movie, and Colleen Hoover’s book on which the movie is based, star Anne Hathaway (who plays the titular character in the film), has her own thoughts. “Letter,” Hathaway tells The Hollywood Reporter when asked if she’s team manuscript or team letter. “The reason that I’m letter, and I know that a lot of people who are team manuscript, they’re like, ‘No, she just wrote the letter to cover her you know what.‘ I’m like, she’s a terrified woman being very, very careful. And this is my thing about the manuscript: There’s a passage where Lowen is describing it, and she’s like, ‘I’ve got to be honest, this book isn’t very good, and it’s really just a lot about sex.’ And she’s just like, ‘I was pretty bored during the next 100 pages,’ but she said how much she was surprised that she liked Verity’s writing, and I think that if Verity really was this no good, villainous, horrible evil murderess that she’s made out to be, don’t you think the book that she would have written about herself would have been excellent ?” Related Stories Beyond the Book Inside the 'Verity' Adaptation: Crafting a Mystery Where Nothing Is Certain Beyond the Book Zoe Kazan on Honoring Steinbeck's 'East of Eden' for Netflix Series While Rethinking Its Characters She adds: “I don’t know. I don’t trust Lowen. I don’t think Lowen’s well, and I think she sees herself as a victim in all situations, and I definitely don’t trust Jeremy. He goes from zero to crazy angry, real fast.” Verity follows Lowen Ashleigh (played by Dakota Johnson ), a struggling writer hired to finish the bestselling book series of renowned author Verity Crawford after an accident leaves her incapacitated. While working at the Crawford home, Lowen discovers a secret manuscript containing Verity’s apparent autobiographical notes, raising disturbing questions about her past and sending her spiraling over what to believe. Josh Hartnett stars as Verity’s husband Jeremy. In a separate interview with THR , Hoover admits her own read of what‘s real has shifted. “When I wrote the book and ended it how I ended it, I was in Lowen’s perspective. It was first-person from Lowen, so I was just as confused as she was, and I’ve carried that with me until recently. I had to read it again for the first time after watching the film, and I think the film influenced me. I’ve actually gained a whole new perspective, and I still don’t know.” Director Michael Showalter isn’t sure where he stands, either. “All the actors have their own version of what they believe is true, and I wanted to honor each of their versions,” he says. “So I’m agnostic.” Verity hit theaters this Friday and nabbed the top spot on the domestic box office chart, earning $32.6 million from 3,510 North American locations. Its budget was $40 million. THR

title: Aaron Sorkin on Why Mark Zuckerberg Isn’t a Villain in ‘The Social Reckoning,’ Despite That “He’s Making Bad Decisions That Are Hurting Us”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Abbey White Plus Icon Abbey White Contributing Writer View All October 5, 2026 10:28am Aaron Sorkin attends 'The Social Reckoning' world premiere at Regal Union Square on Oct. 4 in New York City. Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images Aaron Sorkin knows the way he wrote Mark Zuckerberg in The Social Network may not have always landed exactly as he intended. “We were surprised after The Social Network came out that there were two reactions to Mark, split along generational lines,” Sorkin told The Hollywood Reporter Sunday night at the New York premiere of his new film The Social Reckoning . “If you were a little bit older, you saw it as a cautionary tale, which is what it was intended to be. If you were a little bit younger, surprisingly, you saw it as an inspirational story. ‘Oh wow, I can drop out of school and have an idea and be a billionaire.’” Related Stories Business 'The Social Reckoning' Is an Even Bigger Burn on Mark Zuckerberg Than You Think Movies Jeremy Strong Says He Doesn't "Need to Apologize" for Method Acting: "It's in Service of the Material" “There’s a thing when somebody becomes a billionaire that everybody gets enamored with them, and you’ve got to be like, ‘All right, well, how did you make that money?’” said comedian and actor Bill Burr, who portrays Zuckerberg’s legal counsel in the upcoming film. “I look at [Zuckerberg] as that’s what corporations do. They poison our food supply. They’ve made synthetic heroin. You know those Waymo cars? They’ve killed like 90 people, and they just get a fine. How many people can you kill in a car? They operate with impunity. So as much as this is about social media, it’s about this nerd robber baron era that we’re living in.” In The Social Reckoning , a film Sorkin has described not as a sequel but “as a new movie I wrote pretending I had never written The Social Network ,” who is at the story’s center is noticeably different. This time, the dramatization follows the 2021 Facebook leak, led by former Facebook employee and whistleblower Frances Haugen (played by Mikey Madison) and reported by former Wall Street Journal and current Reuters reporter Jeff Horwitz ( Jeremy Allen White ). For the writer, producer and director, the decision to not do a continuation wasn’t “because I was worried about backlash, and I really didn’t think of it as re-centering or changing anything.” With The Social Reckoning , Haugen and Horwitz become the lens through which this Facebook story is told, while Zuckerberg, portrayed by frequent Sorkin collaborator Jeremy Strong , is a supporting character — the result of what the new film demanded, the filmmaker explained. “It’s not just that he’s older now or that he’s made $120 billion; the company’s worth a trillion dollars and has three billion users. It’s no longer a social media company. It’s no longer about keeping in touch with your friends from school. Now they’ve added a newsfeed, and that newsfeed is run by an algorithm. So you’re getting different news than I’m getting, than he’s getting, than they’re getting. We’re all living in our own world,” Sorkin said. “It gets really hard when we’re looking at our phones, when we’re looking at X and Facebook and Instagram. It’s confusing. I don’t blame people. I blame these companies. It is hard to differentiate. It’s tough, but they know exactly what they’re doing,” emphasized White. “That was the realization I had. I think I gave these companies the benefit of the doubt before I approached this work and started to do the film. I was like, ‘Well, maybe it’s just the genie’s out of the bottle, the monster’s out of the cage. It’s wreaking havoc, and they’ve lost control.’ The truth is, of course they understand exactly what’s going on. It is purposeful. There is intent. They want all of our attention. They want all of our eyes.” For Burr, corporations like Meta that have publicly attributed certain policy choices to free speech protections have come to exemplify how “free speech is a sliding scale and certain people have more free speech than other people.” It’s a narrative around Facebook that has grown and shifted in the decade and a half between The Social Network and The Social Reckoning . Bill Burr, Wunmi Mosaku, Jeremy Allen White, Mikey Madison, Jeremy Strong, Betty Gilpin and Aaron Sorkin Sean Zanni/Getty Images for Sony Pictures Entertainment But despite what the leaks revealed about Facebook’s algorithms, what Zuckerberg and the company’s leadership knew about their impacts and even the fact that “Meta’s lawyers, when they found out about this movie, sent Sony a strongly worded letter ,” according to Sorkin, both the filmmaker and Sony boss Tom Rothman don’t see the tech mogul necessarily as a bad guy or villain. “I wouldn’t, and I don’t think Aaron would use that characterization. I think what has happened in the many years since that first film — that was the dawn of social media — is that anyone would have or could have foreseen that there would be as many ills as good. So now the world is wrestling with the ills of social media, and it’s storytellers’ jobs to confront the problems in our world,” Rothman told THR ahead of the premiere. “I’m a free speech absolutist too, but I know you can’t yell ‘fire!’ in a crowded theater. I know that there is a difference between free speech and falsehood.” “He’s making bad decisions that are hurting us,” added Sorkin. “But in dramatist terms, he’s not a villain. He’s an antihero. A villain has bad intentions. They want the money, they want revenge, that kind of thing. An antihero, the intentions are good: ‘I want to connect everybody in the world.’ But the way an antihero goes about doing it, the decisions they ultimately make are bad.” How Sorkin wanted to portray Zuckerberg is present in Strong’s performance and aligns with the actor’s general approach to playing characters audiences have seen as both antiheroes and villains. “Aaron is always examining the fault lines in our society, and I’ve been interrogating those things, but he’s a writer like Mozart is a composer. He’s that good,” the actor told THR on the carpet. “All I can do is try to be as accurate and truthful as I can and take responsibility for that in what I’m rendering, in the person that I’m rendering, and certainly not set out to vilify him. I’m not interested in making judgments.” In terms of how he worked to inhabit Zuckerberg — a role The Social Network star Jesse Eisenberg turned down after no longer wanting to be associated with the character and person — Strong noted that Sorkin’s writing played a pivotal role in how he was able to “take a piece of material and internalize it.” But he also had “to do an immense amount of work preparing to walk onto that set and to be inside a life , to be totally dialed into it, so that it’s a second skin and that I believe in what I’m doing.” “And it’s absurd. What we do is absurd. I’m not Mark Zuckerberg, right? But my job for the time I make this movie is to believe that I am with authority. And that requires a great deal of concentration — which I think people project all kinds of nonsense onto — and a lot of trust between Aaron and I,” he continued. “And Aaron extends me an immense amount of trust, so I think my job is to meet that trust with as much courage as I can muster and be willing to go way the fuck out on a limb and maybe go up in flames. That’s the risk I have to take. When he asked me to do this one, Sarah Polley wrote a book recently called Run Towards the Danger, and that’s what I have to do: run towards the danger.” With the potential of lawsuits from Facebook and Zuckerberg, the whole film may be doing that alongside Strong. According to Sorkin, “We’ve all been concerned, but the lawyers are there to act as a shield.” “What Hollywood has done occasionally, not in the beginning, but certainly since the ’50s and the ’60s, is played its part in speaking truth to power,” added Rothman. “That’s what this film does, and that’s why we’re proud of it.” The Social Reckoning hits theaters on Friday.
